Like a lot of people I approached Survivalism as a way to prepare for the unknown and unexpected emergencies that seem to randomly strike people. I did all the things that people do and made the decisions that people make.

Do I hunker down and stay in place do I bug out?

If hunker down how much food and water do I need and how long will it last? Do I have space enough for the supplies I need? If I hunker down what do I do for energy and how do I hide my finite energy resources from prying eyes? How do I protect what I have from neighbors who have nothing or a government that now has no resources to support massive population and begins search and confiscation?

If I plan to bug out, where do I go? If I have a place to go what are the resources that the travel requires to get there? Will I have to engage in armed conflict to protect my finite resources to get where I want to go. When I get there and how can I be sure that when I arrive there aren't a thousand other people there all ready and have depleted the resources necessary for survival.

So many questions and so few answer's. So being that I made my living by being an engineer i approached the problem from an engineering perspective. Hunkering down made sense for only a relative short period of time 30 to 40 day max and then what? Bugging out problems were just a daunting. Where do I go? How do I get there? What will be the resources for required to survive during transit to get there? How many people will be there when I get there? Will there be sufficient resources at the bug out site to sustain the population when I get there?

Well in a lot of respects the decision was made for me. The company I worked for (made Oil field and Petroleum refinery equipment) moved a lot of the manufacturing to Mexico so they could do business with countries that the US had sanctions on. The the company brought in 250 Mechanical, Chemical and Petroleum engineers from foreign countries on H2B visas. It was time to hit the road jack. (Relocate I think they call it.) Since I was going to be moving why not move to an area that had a much higher survival factor if the shit hit the fan. All so every company that was interested in me as an employee was in an industry that was dying or would be moving overseas with in 10 years. This required me to rethink my professional objectives.

At a family gathering one thanks giving I over heard a conversation about some one they knew bought some land in the high desert in the Inland United States and took a big hair cut. The land was essentially worthless as it was only good for cattle grazing and could not do much of that. That got me interested in maybe I could get some land dirt cheap, improve it sufficiently that it could provide the resources for a small family to live on. Then I wouldn't have to worry about the company I worked for downsizing or moving off shore.

So I took the plunge and bought some land in the butt end of no where. The land had water rights but there was dammed little water to have a right to in most years. That's why the land was next to worthless and was always on being taken by the state and sold for unpaid back taxes. The plot of land (180 acres) was at the end of a 20 mile dirt road that went no where else. The nearest village (so small the entry and leaving sign on the same post if you can believe it) was 40 miles away. There was no Power or telephone service. It was surrounded by BLM (Federal Government land) and really remote. Nearest neighbor was 20 miles at the beginning of the dirt road.

When I finally got to visit the property I found some fallen down buildings, a wrecked trailer house and a old dilapidated Regulator wind mill that drove a lift pump. There was also a old Aermotor wind mill that used to have a generator on it but some one had stolen the generator. In one of the fallen down building was a battery bank of Nickle Iron batteries that had been tipped over and shot up and just generally destroyed. The north end of the property was at a higher elevation with a basalt rock out cropping that some one had made a small cave in for storage I suppose. At the base of the outcropping was the stream bed of a intermittent spring that was bone dry.The base of the The Regulator Wind mill was on top of the outcropping and a well had been drilled through the rock to what ever water existed down below. The Aeromotor wind mill was also on top of the rock outcropping and that was it.

Well the price was right so I bought the property with the Idea of improving it on week ends and holidays while working in the big city. The first thing I did was re-drill the well and added an additional 250 feet to the shaft. I had to go to a 3/4 inch lift rod on the lift pump to support the extra 250 feet of lift rod. The water lift pump was a solid bronze pump. It had a ball check valve at the bottom of the cylinder and a ball check valve at the top of the piston. On the down stroke the piston force the water below the piston through the check valve ports in the piston to top of the piston On the up stroke the water above the piston was forced out of the piston cylinder up the pipe that supported the lift rod to the surface. The up stroke all so drew water into the bottom of the piston cylinder through the ball check valve at the bottom of the cylinder. The whole thing was driven by the wind mill through a gear box that decreased the speed of the lift to the force necessary to move the water to the surface. At the surface the water was collected in a tank. I soon leaned that I had to bury and hide the tank in the rock out cropping to keep shit head from shooting at it or running it dry. The next Issue was the electric power system. I found out that Nickle Iron batteries are all most indestructible. All I had to do was patch the cases put in the potassium hydroxide at the proper PH and 9 out of the 10 batteries came back on line with no appearing ill effects. God only know how long they had laid in the dirt with out any electrolyte. Oh also placed the batteries in rock cave that was in the basalt rock outcropping. Sine Nickle Iron batteries don't vent any fumes it was a no brainer. I rocked up the entrance to the cave and made a top entry that could now be hidden by other rocks and dirt piled on the trap door.

So now I had power and water to my property,. (very limited amounts to be sure) but now I had the bug. Well a few years passed along with some land swap deals with the BLM (other small plots of worthless land that I improved and then swapped with the BLM for land bordering my property) and I had enough land to make living out here possible. With the drop in prices of Micro wave communications I was able to even set up a computer network on the place.

So I went from a mechanical/Petroleum engineer to a farmer and rancher in the butt end of no where at the end of a 20 mile dirt road that can be easily blocked to wheeld traffic (including bicycle and motor cycles).

So now I don't even worry about survivalism as i am living the survivalist life.
Survivalism not a a prepairation but as a way of life.
